attachments.origin_landmark: floor of the orbit, lateral to the nasolacrimal groove
attachments.insertion_landmark: inferolateral sclera, posterior to the equator

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: True insertion is onto the sclera of the eyeball, not a fixed bony point; the eyeball is not modeled as its own rigid body with rotational DOF in this pass (a natural candidate for a small future extension), so this muscle's insertion is given relative to the orbital bone frame as an engineering approximation of its resting position rather than a moving attachment.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

motor_endplate_zones.reference_line_to: origin (orbital floor, lateral to the nasolacrimal groove)
motor_endplate_zones.notes: The oculomotor nerve branch enters IO near the middle of the muscle and its root-like intramuscular arborization (covering ~7.6mm of a ~30.0mm-long muscle) extends toward the insertion, finishing around the boundary of the distal third of the muscle -- i.e. roughly the middle third of IO's length carries the motor endplates. IO is also the extraocular muscle most directly and most often injected clinically.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Shin HJ, Lee SH, Ha TJ, Song WC, Koh KS, 'Intramuscular Nerve Distribution of the Inferior Oblique Muscle', Curr Eye Res 45(2):215-220 (2019), doi:10.1080/02713683.2019.1662055 (https://doi.org/10.1080/02713683.2019.1662055) -- 72 IO specimens, Sihler staining -- retrieved via PubMed

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Trans-conjunctival, EMG- or landmark-guided injection: the globe is rotated into adduction and elevation (or steadied with forceps) to expose the inferotemporal bulbar conjunctiva, and a needle is passed through the conjunctiva over IO's known course beneath the inferolateral rectus/lateral canthus region, directly into the muscle belly; some centers add EMG confirmation via manual globe rotation, others inject by direct visualization alone under brief general anesthesia in children.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Immediately deep to the inferotemporal bulbar conjunctiva/Tenon's capsule, superficial to the orbital floor periosteum.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: In the EMG-guided technique, discharge increasing with attempted extorsion/elevation-in-adduction (IO's action) confirms placement; in the trans-conjunctival pediatric technique the muscle is often directly visualized.
structures_at_risk: inferior rectus, whose lateral border IO crosses obliquely just deep to it
inferior oblique's own neurovascular pedicle and the inferior vortex vein, which run near the muscle's posterior third
globe perforation if the needle is advanced beyond the thin muscle belly
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Two real technique variants: an EMG-guided percutaneous/trans-conjunctival approach in cooperative adults (used, for example, to simulate an inferior oblique myectomy before committing to surgery), and a simpler trans-conjunctival injection without EMG guidance (a fixed 5 units) commonly used under brief anesthesia in children with inferior oblique overaction. Guidance is EMG or direct visualization, not ultrasound, in real clinical practice.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Norbury C, Shah H, Marsh I, 'Is inferior oblique botulinum toxin injection an effective surgical simulator prior to inferior oblique myectomy? A 30-year retrospective review', Strabismus 33(3):166-173 (2025), doi:10.1080/09273972.2025.2452623 (https://doi.org/10.1080/09273972.2025.2452623) -- 68 patients, EMG-guided technique by a single surgeon; AlQahtani G, Sesma G, AlMesfer S, Alhaimi F, 'Efficacy of botulinum toxin injection in treating primary inferior oblique overaction', Eur J Ophthalmol 36(4):1048-1053 (2026), doi:10.1177/11206721251414695 (https://doi.org/10.1177/11206721251414695) -- 42 eyes, trans-conjunctival technique in children -- both retrieved via PubMed
